content: We report an artificial monooxygenase system that drives enantioselective oxidation directly utilizing molecular oxygen under visible‐light irradiation. This biohybrid catalyst consists of noncatalytic protein and metal complexes, i.e., copper 4,4‐tetraaza‐29H,31H phthalocyanine (CuTPC) bound to bovine serum albumin (BSA) and then assembled onto a synthetic photocatalyst, graphitic carbon nitride (g‐C 3 N 4 ). The resulting hybrid system facilitates a photocatalytic reaction cascade to enable enantioselective oxidation using molecular oxygen as an oxidant: g‐C 3 N 4 reduces oxygen photocatalytically and produces H 2 O 2 , which subsequently activates CuTPC‐BSA to drive enantioselective oxidation reactions. Using styrene and propionic acid as model substrates, the photocatalytic system selectively produces R‐styrene oxide and L‐lactic acid, respectively, achieving enantiomeric excesses exceeding 99% under visible‐light irradiation. In contrast, g‐C 3 N 4 alone did not provide enantioselectivity. Thus, CuTPC‐BSA/g‐C 3 N 4 represents a promising and cost‐effective alternative to natural enzymes to produce chiral oxidation products in a much sustainable way.

title: Sol–Gel Assisted Synthesis of Ca‐Modified α‐ Fe 2 O 3 Films for Enhanced Dye Photodegradation
summary: ABSTRACT This study investigates the synthesis of Ca‐modified hematite (Ca X ‐Fe 2 O 3 ) films via a sol–gel dip‐coating method for visible‐light‐driven photocatalytic applications. The properties of the films were systematically characteri
content: ABSTRACT This study investigates the synthesis of Ca‐modified hematite (Ca X ‐Fe 2 O 3 ) films via a sol–gel dip‐coating method for visible‐light‐driven photocatalytic applications. The properties of the films were systematically characterized using comprehensive analytical techniques. XRD analysis confirmed the formation of a rhombohedral phase with a (104) preferred orientation and a maximum crystallite size of 65 nm, while SEM revealed increased grain agglomeration at higher Ca contents. Optical analyses showed a reduction in the bandgap from 2.10 to 1.96 eV with increasing Ca content, whereas photoluminescence revealed a marked decrease in emission intensity for the 5 wt.% Ca‐modified film, indicating suppressed electron–hole recombination. The 5 wt.% Ca‐modified hematite exhibited significantly enhanced photocatalytic performance, achieving 97% dye degradation within 120 min compared with 64.1% for Fe 2 O 3 . This enhanced activity is attributed to the combined effects of improved visible‐light absorption and efficient charge separation arising from Ca‐induced defect states within the bandgap. Reusability tests demonstrated that the photocatalyst retained approximately 85% of its degradation efficiency after three consecutive monthly photocatalytic cycles, while post‐reaction analyses further confirmed its structural stability after repeated use. These results demonstrate that Ca‐modified Fe 2 O 3 is a promising visible‐light photocatalyst for the sustainable removal of organic pollutants from wastewater.

title: Influence of controlled and modified atmosphere on postharvest quality and physiology of ‘Zes008’ kiwifruit A thesis presented in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy in Food technology at Massey University, Palmerston North, New Zealand
summary: ‘Zes008’ (Actinidia chinensis var. chinensis) is a recently developed kiwifruit cultivar in New Zealand, notable for its red flesh colour and high sweetness. However, its rapid ripening and short storage life in the regular cool chain creat
content: ‘Zes008’ (Actinidia chinensis var. chinensis) is a recently developed kiwifruit cultivar in New Zealand, notable for its red flesh colour and high sweetness. However, its rapid ripening and short storage life in the regular cool chain create challenges for export and supply chain management. To extend the storage life of ‘Zes008’, multiple controlled and modified atmosphere technologies with reduced oxygen (O2) and elevated carbon dioxide (CO2) were evaluated in this study. A range of controlled atmosphere (CA) conditions were tested over 8 weeks of cool storage and subsequent shelf life. An optimal CA condition for maintaining the firmness of ‘Zes008’ was identified. However, CA would be challenging to achieve under sea freight conditions. In addition, rapid softening during retail display conditions also represented a risk of resulting in a poor consumer experience. Modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) as an alternative to CA storage has higher flexibility, as MAP can travel with the fruit through the whole cool chain and maintain a relatively stable atmosphere. With a potential commercial solution of MAP for kiwifruit, a beneficial atmosphere was created. However, ethylene accumulated in the MAP, cancelling the benefits. Additionally, during the subsequent shelf life, retail MAP did not sufficiently maintain fruit quality, substantially differently to previous attempts. On-shore storage under CA conditions, followed by standard shipping and lower retail temperatures, was proposed as a potential pathway to extend shelf life, with the continued risk of rapid softening when temperature control is removed. The changing of CA to regular air and the breaking of cool chain may contribute to the rapid softening in the post-CA stage. Fruit physiology and gene expression were studied during and after CA storage. A physiology study showed that ‘Zes008’ exhibited a different ethylene production pattern from other well-studied kiwifruit cultivars. Specifically, ‘Zes008’ produces detectable ethylene throughout the entire postharvest period, with peaks in ethylene production at the beginning of cool storage, after being shifted out of CA, and by the time the flesh firmness is low. In addition, qPCR results illustrated that the expression of ripening genes was impacted by both atmospheric change and temperature change. Overall, the combination of CA storage onshore and MAP with ethylene management in sea freight may effectively delay the ripening and softening of ‘Zes008’ and offers opportunities to extend storage life. With reduced retail temperature, the marketing window may be further extended and the consumer experience further guaranteed.

title: Studying Protein-Ligand Interactions with In-droplet Hydrogen-Deuterium Exchange Mass Spectrometry and Molecular Dynamics Simulations
summary: Native mass spectrometry (nMS) has been widely used for the characterization of biomolecules and their interactions with ligands under near-physiological conditions, yet connecting the change in conformational dynamics of proteins upon liga
content: Native mass spectrometry (nMS) has been widely used for the characterization of biomolecules and their interactions with ligands under near-physiological conditions, yet connecting the change in conformational dynamics of proteins upon ligand binding remains challenging. In this work, the integration of capillary vibrating sharp-edge spray ionization based-nMS, in-droplet hydrogen deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provides a platform to characterize ligand binding and ligand-induced conformational changes of bovine carbonic anhydrase II (BCAII) upon interaction with its inhibitor, acetazolamide (AZM). cVSSI-based-nMS preserves the protein native-like state and facilitates the direct identification and determination of the apparent binding affinity of the BCAII-AZM complex. In-droplet HDX-MS measurements show a reduction in deuterium incorporation upon AZM binding suggesting ligand-induced structural stabilization of the holo BCAII. MD simulations of the apo and holo protein revealed ligand-induced suppression in backbone fluctuations and enhanced structural rigidity. A new model that uses protection factors (PF) and HDX scoring derived from MD trajectories that is based on solvent accessible surface area (SASA) and hydrogen bonding propensity is further refined. The model reflects experimentally observed trends in deuterium incorporation and offers atomic-level insight into structural stabilization of BCAII upon AZM binding. The combination of the cVSSI-based nMS, in-droplet HDX-MS and MD simulations provides a framework for identification and quantification of protein-ligand interactions and elucidation of ligand-induced changes in conformational dynamics of the protein.

title: A Stable Thioxanthene Dioxide Radical Motif for Modular Access to High‐Spin Diradical and Fully‐Fused Tetraradicaloid Scaffold
summary: ABSTRACT Open‐shell π‐conjugated systems are of fundamental interest due to their fascinating electronic and magnetic properties, yet their rational construction remains challenging. Herein, we report a cyano‐terminated thioxanthene dioxide
content: ABSTRACT Open‐shell π‐conjugated systems are of fundamental interest due to their fascinating electronic and magnetic properties, yet their rational construction remains challenging. Herein, we report a cyano‐terminated thioxanthene dioxide radical ( MR ) as a robust building block for constructing complex di‐/tetraradical architectures. The MR motif features a sulfone‐fused, quasi‐planar core that, synergized by electron‐withdrawing para ‐cyano groups, provides significant thermodynamic stabilization to yield an exceptional ambient half‐life time ( t 1/2 ) of 81 days. Leveraging this scaffold, we achieved the modular synthesis of an m ‐phenylene‐bridged diradical ( DR ) and a fully‐fused tetraradicaloid ( TR ) via a high‐efficiency radical‐mediated oxidative cyclization protocol. While DR represents a rare air‐stable triplet‐ground‐state diradical (Δ E S‐T = 0.13 kcal/mol), the tetraradicaloid TR possesses a singlet ground state stabilized by global aromaticity across its π‐core, accompanied by an unconventional energy hierarchy featuring a quintet manifold as the lowest thermally accessible excited state. Notably, TR demonstrates excellent room‐temperature spin coherence, with spin‐lattice relaxation/spin dephasing time ( T 1 /T 2 ) of 85.47/1.17 µs, suggesting its good potential as robust spin qubits under ambient conditions. These results establish MR as a versatile radical motif for developing complex multi‐spin systems with emergent magnetic/quantum information functionalities.

title: Light-Driven Electron-Transfer Catalysis on Earth-Abundant CuFeS2 Nanocrystals Probed by Operando SERS
summary: Plasmonic nanoparticles possess a strong optical absorption but suffer from low catalytic activity and limited sustainability. Here, we demonstrate that earth-abundant chalcopyrite CuFeS2 nanocrystals (NCs) can serve as a dual-functional pl
content: Plasmonic nanoparticles possess a strong optical absorption but suffer from low catalytic activity and limited sustainability. Here, we demonstrate that earth-abundant chalcopyrite CuFeS2 nanocrystals (NCs) can serve as a dual-functional platform benefitting from a strong polaritonic absorption enabling surfaceenhanced Raman scattering (SERS), and providing at the same time high activity for light-induced electrontransfer catalysis. The nanocrystals exhibit a prominent optical resonance at 500 nm, originating from interband transitions into a Fe 3d derived intermediate band that drives the dielectric function toward the Fröhlich condition. This localized resonance yields a SERS analytical enhancement factor of ~ 3×103 for 1,2-bis(4-pyridyl)ethylene (BPE), validated by Discontinuous Galerkin Time-Domain (DGTD) electrodynamic simulations and Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations that motivates synergistic near-field and charge transfer contributions. In addition, the CuFeS2 NCs efficiently drive the selective photoconversion of p-nitrothiophenol (NTP) to 4,4′-dimercaptoazobenzene (DMAB). Crucially, wavelength-dependent SERS and kinetic measurements prove that both Raman amplification and surface reactivity follow the optical resonance profile. Power-dependent and substrate-heating controls further confirm that this reactivity is mediated by photoexcited electron transfer into adsorbate orbitals rather than photothermal heating. By integrating a polaritonic optical enhancement with long excited state lifetimes provided by the intermediate band electronic structure in a single earth-abundant material, this work establishes CuFeS2 nanocrystals as a versatile architecture for SERS diagnostics and non-thermal photochemistry.

title: Fluorine-Free Gas Diffusion Media for Polymer Electrolyte Fuel Cells Part I: Silicone-based Microporous Layers
summary: The widespread use of fluoropolymers in electrochemical energy systems, coupled with increasing environmental, health, and regulatory concerns surrounding per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), is motivating the development of fluorine
content: The widespread use of fluoropolymers in electrochemical energy systems, coupled with increasing environmental, health, and regulatory concerns surrounding per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), is motivating the development of fluorine-free alternatives. Here, silicone-based resins are evaluated as fluorine-free binders for microporous layers (MPLs) and integrated into fully fluorine-free gas diffusion media (GDMs). Using Sylgard 184 silicone elastomer, the binder content was systematically varied, identifying 25 wt.% as the lowest loading that provided sufficient water repellency. At this loading, the influence of binder chemistry was investigated by replacing Sylgard 184 with KR-220L, a methyl silicone rigid resin. Although the resin chemistry strongly affected MPL thickness, porosity, and crack formation, its impact on fuel-cell performance was limited. Fully fluorinefree GDMs were then fabricated by depositing silicone-based MPLs onto carbon fiber substrates hydrophobized via organosilicon electrografting. Replacing a commercial PTFEtreated substrate with the fluorine-free electrografted substrate resulted in only a minor decrease in current density, from 4.2 to 4.0 A cm-2 at 0.3 V under high-humidity conditions; both exceeded the commercial fluorinated reference (3.8 A cm-2). Accelerated stress testing further demonstrated promising durability. Overall, silicone-based materials represent a viable route toward replacing fluorinated components in GDMs.

title: Sustainable forage crop production systems for fodder security: A review
summary: Livestock farming significantly contributes to India's agricultural sector by supporting rural livelihoods, food and nutritional security, employment and sustainable farming practices. India supports approximately 536.7 million livestock; h
content: Livestock farming significantly contributes to India's agricultural sector by supporting rural livelihoods, food and nutritional security, employment and sustainable farming practices. India supports approximately 536.7 million livestock; however, only about 4 % of its cultivable land is devoted to fodder production, resulting in a persistent shortage of quality feed resources. The fodder demand–supply gap has widened due to limited land available for fodder cultivation, degradation of grazing lands, competition with food crops and limited access to improved fodder technologies. Irregular rainfall, droughts and declining forage productivity and quality have further exacerbated these challenges under changing climatic conditions. Reliance on low-quality crop residues and inadequate feed preservation practices adversely affects animal health, livestock productivity and farmers' income. This review synthesises recent advances in sustainable forage production systems, fodder conservation technologies and climate-resilient strategies to identify approaches for improving fodder security and resilient livestock production. It examines the role of quality fodder in improving the efficiency of current livestock production systems by enhancing milk production, reproductive performance and feed-use efficiency, while identifying key challenges, including weak forage seed systems, inadequate extension services and limited policy support. The review concludes that diversified forage systems, improved fodder conservation practices, rehabilitation of grazing resources and integrated crop–livestock systems are essential for strengthening fodder security and ensuring sustainable livestock production in India.

title: Metabolite co-variation networks reveal keystone functions and an emergent pathogen state in the human urobiome.
summary: Microbial communities are dynamic, adaptive ecosystems whose collective behavior emerges from metabolic interactions such as cross-feeding, competition, and cooperation, rather than taxonomic diversity or individual metabolic potential alon
content: Microbial communities are dynamic, adaptive ecosystems whose collective behavior emerges from metabolic interactions such as cross-feeding, competition, and cooperation, rather than taxonomic diversity or individual metabolic potential alone. This distinction is clinically significant in the postmenopausal urinary tract, where recurrent urinary tract infections (rUTIs) are associated with complex, persistent infection dynamics including multiple contributing bacterial species. The ability of resident microbial communities to prevent pathogen establishment, known as colonization resistance, is increasingly attributed to the metabolic interactions within the urobiome itself rather than any single resident species. However, current approaches, such as taxonomic profiling and classical differential abundance analysis, can only partially describe the presence or maintenance of such interactions. Consequently, the community-level metabolic architecture determining pathogen resistance remains incompletely understood. To address this gap, we developed PhenoRewire, a network-based framework that quantifies how metabolite co-variation is rewired between biological states using untargeted metabolomics data. We applied this framework to an induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) urothelial organoid-derived barrier co-cultured with synthetic urobiome communities as a model of urobiome-pathogen dynamics relevant to rUTIs in two approaches. In an infection model, clinically isolated uropathogens Escherichia coli and Enterococcus faecalis, were co-cultured with a three-member urobiome community consisting of Lactobacillus gasseri, Lactobacillus crispatus, and Gardnerella vaginalis. Here we show how E. coli drove the metabolic reorganization, while E. faecalis amplified it disproportionately. PhenoRewire disentangled the 6-fold metabolic network amplification mediated by E. faecalis as a metabolic facilitator, revealing an emergent urobiome-pathogen co-variation architecture (1,781 vs 227 edges) not recapitulated by either community alone. Moreover, in a six-member urobiome single-strain dropout experiment, we revealed that removal of the sole Actinomycete Winkia anitrata caused significant network collapse (Louvain modularity falls from 0.707 to 0.038), identifying it as the single non-redundant keystone of the community. More broadly, these results demonstrate how untargeted metabolomics co-variation network analysis can be applied to defined synthetic urobiomes in combination with a urothelial host model to elucidate community dynamics. This framework provides a template that can be extended beyond the urobiome to investigate any complex microbial community where ecological behavior remains an open question.

title: Systematic Evaluation of Concrete Placement Reliability in Heavily Reinforced Nuclear Structures
source: International Journal of Concrete Structures and Materials
summary: Concrete placement in nuclear power plant (NPP) structures is challenged by severe reinforcement congestion and complex internal geometries, where conventional slump-based workability control may not reliably predict placement performance.
content: Concrete placement in nuclear power plant (NPP) structures is challenged by severe reinforcement congestion and complex internal geometries, where conventional slump-based workability control may not reliably predict placement performance. This study investigates the relationship between polycarboxylate ether-based admixture (PCE) adsorption, rheological behavior, and placement performance through a multiscale experimental program. Conventional workability tests (slump, L-box, and U-box), PCE adsorption analysis using total organic carbon (TOC), rheological characterization, and custom-fabricated placement simulation tests were performed. The results showed that mixtures with similar slump values exhibited significantly different passing behavior due to differences in PCE adsorption and resulting rheological properties. A clear relationship between yield stress and blockage risk was identified using a vertical drop test, indicating that mixtures with paste yield stress exceeding approximately 0.3 Pa exhibited reduced discharge and a high risk of blockage under reinforced congestion. A horizontal filling test further demonstrated that horizontal placement represents a more severe condition than vertical passing, as even highly flowable concrete could not achieve complete void-free filling along extended horizontal paths under self-weight.

title: Stabilization of Metastable 2D Wurtzite MnS via Sulfur Vacancy Engineering
summary: ABSTRACT Metastable wurtzite transition‐metal compounds are of interest because their hexagonal symmetry can enable electronic and magnetic behaviors inaccessible to thermodynamically stable phases. Their synthesis in the 2D limit, however,
content: ABSTRACT Metastable wurtzite transition‐metal compounds are of interest because their hexagonal symmetry can enable electronic and magnetic behaviors inaccessible to thermodynamically stable phases. Their synthesis in the 2D limit, however, remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate the direct growth of metastable 2D wurtzite MnS nanosheets by atmospheric‐pressure chemical vapor deposition via sulfur‐vacancy engineering. Ultrathin MnS nanosheets with lateral dimensions of tens of micrometers are grown in a 10 min deposition step. Phase selection is controlled by the cooling atmosphere: interrupting the gas flow after growth creates sulfur‐deficient conditions, promotes sulfur‐vacancy formation, and stabilizes the wurtzite phase, whereas continuous flow supply yields the stable rock‐salt phase. Transmission electron microscopy and grazing‐incidence wide‐angle X‐ray scattering confirm the wurtzite structure, and electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy reveals abundant sulfur vacancies. The nanosheets exhibit p ‐type semiconducting transport, negative magnetoresistance up to room temperature, and a low‐temperature exchange‐bias effect. These results identify sulfur vacancies as a key determinant of metastable phase stabilization and provide a design principle that may be extendable to other chalcogenide systems.

title: Liquid Crystal Elastomers Micro‐Supercapacitors with Robust Interfacial Integration for Untethered Soft Robotics
summary: ABSTRACT Untethered integrated energy‐actuation systems are desirable for soft robots to break their long‐standing dependence on external power tethers. However, it remains challenging to develop stable functional modules with robust interf
content: ABSTRACT Untethered integrated energy‐actuation systems are desirable for soft robots to break their long‐standing dependence on external power tethers. However, it remains challenging to develop stable functional modules with robust interfacial integrity that endure repetitive actuation without delamination. Herein, we report thermally driven micro‐supercapacitor (TD‐MSC) soft modules fabricated via direct ink writing of MXene/ TEMPO‐oxidized bacterial cellulose (TOBC) electrodes on plasma‐activated liquid crystal elastomers (LCEs). A strong dual‐coupled interface with synergistic non‐covalent and covalent bonding is constructed via a trimethylolpropane tris(3‐mercaptopropionate) (TMPTMP) and trimethylolpropane triacrylate (TMPTA) click chemistry‐based electrolyte. The resulting TD‐MSCs deliver an areal capacitance of 106.12 mF cm − 2 and retain 69% capacitance after 5000 cycles, benefiting from TOBC‐enabled ion transport pathways and enhanced mechanical integrity. The device achieves controllable, reversible thermally‐driven deformation, enabling biomimetic peristalsis motion while maintaining robust interfacial bonding and stable electrochemical performance. Importantly, distinct actuation modules can be realized by tailoring the spatial arrangement of the electrodes. As a proof‐of‐concept illustration, untethered integrated soft systems with onboard energy storage capable of heavy‐duty grasping and state sensing are constructed by integrating TD‐MSCs with thermally responsive control circuits. This work demonstrates an integrated energy‐actuation architecture and provides a promising strategy for multifunctional soft robotic systems with environmental interaction.

title: 4.8 V and All‐Climate (−60 to 55°C) All‐Solid‐State Batteries Enabled by Dual‐Phase Symbiotic Halide Solid Electrolytes
summary: ABSTRACT Overcoming the intrinsic trade‐off between high‐voltage compatibility, thermal stability, and low‐temperature ionic conductivity in halide solid electrolytes remains a critical challenge for advancing all‐solid‐state lithium batter
content: ABSTRACT Overcoming the intrinsic trade‐off between high‐voltage compatibility, thermal stability, and low‐temperature ionic conductivity in halide solid electrolytes remains a critical challenge for advancing all‐solid‐state lithium batteries (ASSLBs). Here, we propose a chemical symbiosis strategy to design a dual‐phase halide electrolyte integrating nanocrystalline LiAlCl 4 with amorphous Li‐M‐O‐Cl (M = Ta/Al) phases. This innovative architecture synergistically combines the ultra‐high‐voltage stability (up to 4.8 V) of the crystalline phase with the low‐energy‐barrier ion transport pathways in the amorphous matrix. The designed electrolyte exhibits exceptional electrochemical performance under extreme conditions. It enables the ASSLBs to achieve a 90.5% capacity retention after 100 cycles at 4.8 V, maintain a specific capacity of 133 mA h g −1 over 500 cycles at 55 °C and 3 C, and deliver unprecedented low‐temperature performance with a capacity of 109.6 mA h g −1 and 1800‐h stability under dual extreme conditions of −60°C and 4.8 V. Comprehensive characterization reveals the amorphous phase facilitates facile percolation networks for rapid Li + conduction, while the nanocrystalline domains maintain structural integrity against high‐voltage degradation. The electrolyte's broad compatibility with diverse cathodes (LiCoO 2 , LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 ) also underscores its versatility for high‐energy ASSLBs.

title: Nadifloxacin: Multimilligram Enantioresolution and Enantioselective Ecotoxicological Studies
summary: ABSTRACT Emerging contaminants are an increasing global concern, with antibiotics representing a notable case due to their continuous release and possible contribution to antimicrobial resistance. Fluoroquinolones (FQs) combine high stabili
content: ABSTRACT Emerging contaminants are an increasing global concern, with antibiotics representing a notable case due to their continuous release and possible contribution to antimicrobial resistance. Fluoroquinolones (FQs) combine high stability, low biodegradability, and biological activity at trace levels, which result in persistence, ecotoxicity, and bioaccumulation in aquatic systems. Nadifloxacin (NAD) is a chiral FQ prescribed as a racemate for dermatological infections, but ( S )‐NAD is more potent than the racemate and 64 to 256 times more active than ( R )‐NAD against both Staphylococcus aureus and Propionibacterium acnes , as well as other gram‐positive and gram‐negative pathogens. Though the stereochemistry plays a decisive role in both pharmacological activity and environmental fate, the enantioselective ecotoxicological evaluation of NAD is of high importance. Thus, this work described the enantioseparation of NAD by chiral liquid chromatography (cLC) on a Lux amylose‐1 column (4.6 mm I.D. × 250 mm L, particle size 5 μm) under normal‐phase conditions. Optimized analytical conditions provided good chromatographic parameters ( R s = 5.92, α = 2.77, retention 6–10 min) and were successfully scaled up to semipreparative enantioseparation on a CHIRALPAK AD ‐H DAICEL column (10 mm I.D. × 250 mm L, particle size 5 μm), allowing the separation of both enantiomers in > 98% enantiomeric purity. The absolute configuration and the elution order of the enantiomers were determined by the agreement between the experimental and calculated data of electronic circular dichroism. The acute ecotoxicity of the NAD racemate and its enantiomers was evaluated using Daphnia magna as an aquatic model organism.

title: Starch/PBAT Composite Films With Hybrid Silicates: Structure–Property Relationships and Application in Cherry Modified‐Atmosphere Packaging
summary: ABSTRACT Starch/poly(butylene adipate‐co‐terephthalate) (PBAT) composite films containing dual silicate fillers were fabricated by extrusion blowing for biodegradable modified‐atmosphere packaging (MAP). The combination of diatomite, kaolin
content: ABSTRACT Starch/poly(butylene adipate‐co‐terephthalate) (PBAT) composite films containing dual silicate fillers were fabricated by extrusion blowing for biodegradable modified‐atmosphere packaging (MAP). The combination of diatomite, kaolin and zeolite was associated with a filler‐mediated interfacial network that enhanced mechanical strength, flexibility and transparency while regulating gas‐transport pathways. A steady‐state analysis suggested that the internal CO 2 /O 2 equilibrium depends on the coupling between fruit respiration and film gas selectivity. Among all formulations, the diatomite–zeolite film (D‐Z) exhibited balanced O 2 /CO 2 permeability, low humidity sensitivity and superior structural uniformity, enabling the formation of a stable atmosphere with low O 2 (1.1%) and moderate CO 2 (14.3%) levels. When applied to cherry preservation, the D‐Z film effectively delayed spoilage and maintained fruit quality. This work provides a feasible strategy for designing sustainable, humidity‐tolerant and atmosphere‐regulating bioplastic films for fresh produce packaging.

title: Unveiling Electrode–Electrolyte Interfacial Synergy in CTAB‐Modulated Pd Single‐Atom Catalysts for Efficient H 2 O 2 Electrosynthesis
summary: ABSTRACT The design of high‐activity single‐atom catalysts (SACs) toward two‐electron oxygen reduction is dominated by regulating the adsorption energy of *OOH intermediates at active sites, whereas the critical factor of proton activity at
content: ABSTRACT The design of high‐activity single‐atom catalysts (SACs) toward two‐electron oxygen reduction is dominated by regulating the adsorption energy of *OOH intermediates at active sites, whereas the critical factor of proton activity at the catalyst–electrolyte interface has received insufficient attention. Herein, an electrode–electrolyte synergistic strategy was employed to modulate the electronic structure of Pd single‐atom sites via the construction of a Pd/CeO 2 ‐MXene heterostructure and hydrogen bond strength using cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) additive. X‐ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) and density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed that the real active sites are Pd single‐atom sites anchored via Pd‐O‐Ce bonding, which significantly reduces the free energies of the key reaction steps (H 2 O→*OOH→H 2 O 2 ). In situ attenuated total reflection surface‐enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR‐SEIRAS) further verified that CTAB adsorbed at the reaction interface can enhance the hydrogen bond strength of interfacial water molecules, reduce the supply of interfacial *H species, and thereby effectively suppress H 2 O 2 decomposition. As a result, the Pd/CeO 2 ‐MXene+CTAB system achieves a low electron transfer number of 2.02 and a high H 2 O 2 selectivity of 98.8% at 0.5 V. This study provides a novel insight into the rational design of proton‐coupled electrocatalysts through the integration of interfacial hydrogen bond engineering and single‐atom catalysts.

title: Thermal and Physical Properties of Gummy Candies and Marshmallows Made With Isomaltulose and Allulose
summary: ABSTRACT Rare sugars are becoming increasingly popular as alternatives to sucrose within the confectionery industry. To effectively incorporate them into confections, it is valuable to have a firm understanding of how the rare sugars affect
content: ABSTRACT Rare sugars are becoming increasingly popular as alternatives to sucrose within the confectionery industry. To effectively incorporate them into confections, it is valuable to have a firm understanding of how the rare sugars affect the physicochemical properties of confections. Gummy candies and marshmallows were made using sucrose, and then again, completely replacing the sucrose first with the rare sugar isomaltulose and next with allulose. The candies were imaged with scanning electron microscopy, showing the different crystallization behaviors within the candy matrices. Texture analysis was used to determine cohesiveness, hardness, and gumminess of the candies. Gummy candies made with isomaltulose were harder and less cohesive than those made with sucrose and allulose (hardness values of gummy candies made with Sucrose: 82.8 ± 34.0 N; Isomaltulose: 350.9 ± 40.9 N; Allulose: 26.55 ± 5.7 N). Marshmallows made with allulose were softer and less cohesive than those made with the other sugars. Moisture sorption isotherms were determined, indicating that candies made with isomaltulose remained relatively stable across the range of water activities. Comparatively, allulose had a higher affinity for water within the same storage conditions. Thermal properties were additionally studied. Candies made with allulose regularly had a lower glass transition temperature than those made with the other sugars. Results indicated that the use of isomaltulose and allulose do affect the thermal and physical properties of confections and have different suitability for use.

title: Mueller manoeuvre increases the mitral‐to‐aortic velocity–time integral ratio, a mitral regurgitant index, in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy
summary: Abstract A reduction of intrathoracic pressure during the Mueller manoeuvre (MM) has been shown to decrease left ventricular (LV) forward stroke volume in patients with systolic heart failure. To assess the underlying mechanisms, we analyze
content: Abstract A reduction of intrathoracic pressure during the Mueller manoeuvre (MM) has been shown to decrease left ventricular (LV) forward stroke volume in patients with systolic heart failure. To assess the underlying mechanisms, we analyzed MM‐induced changes in LV inflow and outflow dynamics in 13 healthy individuals (mean age 42 y, 8 men) and in 13 patients with dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) (mean age 44 y, 8 men) having LV ejection fraction <40% without mitral regurgitation. The subjects performed MM with a target of −30 mmHg pressure for >10 s. Doppler echocardiography was used to record systolic and diastolic flow velocities at the aortic and mitral valve annulus, respectively, during quiet respiration and the MM. The respective flow velocity‐time integrals (VTI) were measured. Compared with control subjects, patients with DCM had a larger MM‐induced decrease in the aortic VTI (−4.2 ± 0.3 vs. −1.6 ± 0.5 cm; p < 0.001) combined with a tendency to a smaller decrease in the mitral VTI (−1.4 ± 0.5 vs. –2.2 ± 0.3 cm; p = 0.070). The mitral‐to‐aortic VTI ratio, an indirect mitral regurgitant index, increased in DCM from 0.78 ± 0.04 to 1.03 ± 0.08 ( p = 0.006) but decreased in the control group from 0.70 ± 0.03 to 0.61 ± 0.03 ( p = 0.025). The group x MM interaction was statistically highly significant ( F = 16.8, p < 0.001). We conclude that, in DCM‐related heart failure, a reduction of intrathoracic pressure during the MM increases the mitral‐to‐aortic VTI ratio suggesting appearance of functional mitral regurgitation.

title: Rapid Proton‐Transfer‐Induced Alkylamine Functionalization of MXene for High‐Force Electrochemical Actuators
summary: ABSTRACT Ti 3 C 2 T x MXene films are promising electrodes for low‐voltage supercapacitor‐like electrochemical actuators (ECAs). However, the little intralayer strain and instability of MXene sheets limit the actuation performance and shelf
content: ABSTRACT Ti 3 C 2 T x MXene films are promising electrodes for low‐voltage supercapacitor‐like electrochemical actuators (ECAs). However, the little intralayer strain and instability of MXene sheets limit the actuation performance and shelf life of MXene‐based ECAs. Here we demonstrate that hydrophobic alkylamines, such as tetradecylamine (TDA), readily functionalize MXene sheets via a rapid proton transfer reaction within minutes, simultaneously enhancing both the in‐plane actuation strain and stability of the MXene film. The remarkably improved actuation of the TDA‐functionalized MXene film can be attributed to the higher inter‐edge expansion/contraction of hydrophobic TDA‐MXene sheets enabled by the co‐insertion/extraction of protonated TDA (TDAH + ) ions with hydrated lithium ions. The assembled bending ECA can generate a peak‐to‐peak strain difference of 0.997% under a triangular voltage of ±1 V and a blocking force up to 207 times its weight under DC 1 V. Furthermore, the designed soft tweezer can grasp an object of 20.3 times its weight and then hold it securely under 0 V. This study opens a new avenue for developing high‐performance ECAs.

title: Electrocapillary Metal Expulsion in Ga–Bi–Sn–Pb Liquid Alloy System
summary: ABSTRACT Electrocapillary metal expulsion has recently emerged as a promising low‐temperature approach for separating metals from liquid alloys. However, prior studies have been largely limited to binary and ternary systems in aqueous elect
content: ABSTRACT Electrocapillary metal expulsion has recently emerged as a promising low‐temperature approach for separating metals from liquid alloys. However, prior studies have been largely limited to binary and ternary systems in aqueous electrolytes, where selectivity is primarily governed by intrinsic surface‐energy differences of the constituent solute metals. Here, we extend this framework to a multicomponent quaternary Ga–Bi–Sn–Pb liquid alloy and demonstrate that electrolyte composition provides an additional parameter for controlling expulsion behavior. Under cathodic polarization of the liquid metal–electrolyte interface, electrocapillary charging reduces interfacial tension and promotes surface over‐enrichment (supersaturation), leading to interfacial instability and the expulsion of solute metals as nanoparticles. The expulsion sequence is governed by the combined effects of surface energy and excess Gibbs free energy, following the order Bi → Pb → Sn → Ga in non‐aqueous electrolytes. In contrast, aqueous electrolytes enable selective suppression of Pb expulsion and cation‐dependent control over Bi and Sn separation. By exploiting this electrolyte‐dependent behavior, two protocols are established: a single‐electrolyte approach for rapid preconcentration and a stepwise electrolyte‐switching strategy for high‐purity separation, yielding Bi (>98 wt.%), Sn (∼88–92 wt.%), and Pb (>95 wt.%). This work establishes electrocapillary refining as a low‐temperature tunable platform for selective metal recovery from multicomponent liquid alloys.

title: Achieving ultra-high strength in low-carbon content steel
summary: While martensitic transformation is a fundamental strengthening mechanism in high-carbon steels, its application in low-carbon content alloys is severely restricted by the ultrahigh cooling rates conventionally required to suppress diffusio
content: While martensitic transformation is a fundamental strengthening mechanism in high-carbon steels, its application in low-carbon content alloys is severely restricted by the ultrahigh cooling rates conventionally required to suppress diffusion-controlled phase transformations. Here, we demonstrate that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment effectively bypasses these kinetic limitations, yielding an ultrahigh-strength Fe–0.33 wt.% C steel with a hardness of 860 HV, a compressive yield strength of 3 GPa, and a compressive fracture strain of 25%. This strength–compressive plasticity synergy originates from a hierarchical microstructure composed of micrometer-scale blocks and nanometer-scale laths. Under multi-gigapascal pressures, the thermodynamic T0 and martensite-start (Ms) temperatures are significantly depressed, simultaneously suppressing martensite embryo growth and inhibiting atomic diffusion. As a result, a twin-dominated, single-variant architecture is stabilized even under relatively slow cooling conditions. Subsequent low-temperature annealing relieves processing-induced residual stresses without coarsening these critical nanoscale features. By decoupling phase-transformation kinetics from conventional rapid-quenching constraints, our approach provides a thermodynamic blueprint for designing next-generation high-performance structural alloys.

title: Effect of austenitization temperature on microstructural evolution and mechanical behavior of a Q&P-processed 420J2 martensitic stainless steel
source: Journal of Materials Research and Technology
summary: The mechanical performance of quenching and partitioning (Q&P)-processed martensitic stainless steels is highly sensitive to the stability of retained austenite (RA). In this study, a commercial 420J2 stainless steel was subjected to Q&P pr
content: The mechanical performance of quenching and partitioning (Q&P)-processed martensitic stainless steels is highly sensitive to the stability of retained austenite (RA). In this study, a commercial 420J2 stainless steel was subjected to Q&P processing with austenitization temperatures ranging from 900 to 1200°C, and the resulting microstructural evolution and mechanical behavior were compared with those produced by conventional quenching and tempering (Q&T). Increasing austenitization temperature promoted the dissolution of coarse M 23 C 6 carbides, increased carbon content in the matrix, and increased the fraction of austenite remaining after the first quench. Consequently, the RA fraction increased and reached a maximum value of 0.33 at 1100°C. However, further increasing the austenitization temperature reduced the effectiveness of carbon enrichment during partitioning, resulting in thermally unstable austenite and fresh martensite formation during the final quench. Tensile behavior was governed primarily by austenite stability rather than its fraction. The steel austenitized at 1000°C achieved the optimum tensile strength-ductility combination (1425 MPa and 16%) owing to the gradual transformation of austenite with optimal mechanical stability during deformation. In contrast, 1100Q&P and 1200Q&P exhibited premature martensitic transformation and reduced ductility. These results demonstrate that optimizing retained-austenite stability, rather than maximizing its fraction, is crucial for exploiting the full potential of Q&P processing in martensitic stainless steels.

title: Methylotrophic yeast engineering for secreted protein production via precision fermentation: food ingredient proteins and synthetic biology strategies
summary: Methylotrophic yeasts are outstanding platforms for the production of recombinant proteins through precision fermentation. Growing demand for protein-based food ingredients requires economically viable secretion efficiency and space-time yi
content: Methylotrophic yeasts are outstanding platforms for the production of recombinant proteins through precision fermentation. Growing demand for protein-based food ingredients requires economically viable secretion efficiency and space-time yields, as well as correct post-translational modifications to ensure proper food functionality. Here, we review recent advances and future potential in engineering methylotrophic yeasts for food protein production, with particular focus on Komagataella phaffii. We first summarise the production of three categories of protein food ingredients: recombinant dairy proteins, proteins for plant-based and cultivated meat applications, and sweet-tasting proteins. Addressing the dual goals of improving both yield and quality, we then review synthetic biology and metabolic engineering strategies in methylotrophic yeasts, with emphasis on genome engineering and gene expression tools, protein secretory pathway engineering, and glycoengineering. Further advances in synthetic biology, integrated with industrial process development, will be critical to unlocking future precision fermentation systems based on methylotrophic yeasts.

title: Zeolitic imidazolate framework-67 (ZIF-67)/Prussian blue analogue (PBA) composite-derived Co-Fe mixed metal oxide as efficient bifunctional electrocatalyst for photo-assisted alkaline water electrolysis
summary: A metal organic framework (MOF) derived Co-Fe mixed metal oxide CFP-Z67@T was rationally designed via a one-step hydrothermal synthesis followed by calcination as a bifunctional photo-assisted electrocatalyst for alkaline water electrolysis
content: A metal organic framework (MOF) derived Co-Fe mixed metal oxide CFP-Z67@T was rationally designed via a one-step hydrothermal synthesis followed by calcination as a bifunctional photo-assisted electrocatalyst for alkaline water electrolysis. Unlike conventional Co-Fe oxide and TiO 2 composites, the integration of CoFe-PBA, ZIF-67, and TiO 2 precursors enabled the formation of a porous multiphase composed of Co 3 O 4 , Fe 2 O 3 , CoFe 2 O 4 and TiO 2 . The MOF precursors served as sacrificial templates, preserving a hierarchical porous architecture with abundant exposed active sites and efficient charge transport, while the derived mixed metal oxides acted as the primary electrocatalytic active phases. Under illumination, the charge-transfer resistance of CFP-Z67@T decreased from 18.0 to 13.5 Ω for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and from 10.4 to 10.0 Ω for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), indicating enhanced interfacial charge transfer. Benefiting from the synergistic effects of the multiphase heterostructure and TiO 2 assisted photoexcitation, CFP-Z67@T required only 1.98 V to achieve 100 mA cm -2 . Furthermore, the catalyst maintained stable operation for over 7802 h at 100 mA cm -2 . Transient photocurrent and electrochemical impedance analyses confirmed efficient photogenerated charge separation and accelerated interfacial charge transfer. This work provides a precursor-engineering strategy for developing high performance noble metal free photo assisted electrocatalysts for sustainable hydrogen production.

title: Combined-Cycle Approach Holds Potential for Offshore-Facility Carbon Capture
summary: _ This article, written by JPT Technology Editor Chris Carpenter, contains highlights of paper SPE 225466, “Combined Cycle and Carbon Capture on Offshore Installations: History, Status, and Future,” by Pål Kloster, CTO Energy and Techouse A
content: _ This article, written by JPT Technology Editor Chris Carpenter, contains highlights of paper SPE 225466, “Combined Cycle and Carbon Capture on Offshore Installations: History, Status, and Future,” by Pål Kloster, CTO Energy and Techouse AS. The paper has not been peer-reviewed. _ Floating thermal power plants implementing CO2 capture and storage (CCS) provide clean power and enhanced oil recovery to the offshore oil and gas industry. Some have used combined-cycle technology, in which gas turbines (GTs) and steam turbines (STs) are used together to convert fuel into electricity. The complete paper describes the potential of combined-cycle technology in CCS applications for offshore facilities. Features of Combined Cycle With Exhaust-Gas Recycling (EGR) and CCS Most offshore installations use GTs to power the facility. The process-heat requirement normally is covered by heat recovery from the GT exhaust. The GTs exhibit between 30 and 38% power efficiency and represent approximately 85–95% of CO2 emissions from offshore oil and gas installations. Introducing combined cycles where pressurized steam is produced by heat recovery of the GT exhaust and expanded over an ST will reduce the fuel gas requirements and CO2 emissions by approximately 25%. Probably the most-studied technology to clean CO2 from GT exhaust gas is by using an absorption process based on amines. The size and, consequently, the cost of such a cleaning process is highly dependent on the volume flow of exhaust gas and the percentage of CO2 removed. Before entering the amine absorber, the exhaust gas must be cooled to approximately 35°C. The cooling is performed in direct-contact coolers (DCCs), components normally requiring space separate from the amine plant. A way to reduce the volume flow to the absorber is to recycle cooled exhaust gas to the air intake of the GTs, a process known as EGR. This is possible because GTs run with large amounts of excess air, leaving approximately 13 vol% of oxygen in the exhaust gas. Recycling of a portion of the exhaust gas will replace some of the inlet air flow to the GTs, increase CO2 concentrations, and reduce exhaust flow to the CCS plant. This will reduce the size of the amine absorber and the CCS plant. Designing and arranging the EGR system efficiently will yield a net reduction in investment cost, size, weight, and space requirement. Quantitatively, the EGR flow will be between 40 and 50% of the exhaust gas flow. The result is an approximate doubling of CO2 concentration and 50% reduced flow to the amine absorber. The flow area and the overall weight of the absorber is reduced by 40–50%. History and Current Status Combined Cycles Offshore. The first combined-cycle plants on offshore oil and gas installations were installed in the North Sea in the late 1990s, but they are now operating globally. However, to achieve a 20–25% reduction in fuel gas consumption and CO2 emissions using combined-cycle technology, several hurdles must be overcome

title: Operational Strategies for Reducing the Energy and Carbon Footprint of AI-Enabled Cloud Infrastructure
source: International Journal of Global Innovations and Solutions (IJGIS)
summary: As workloads in artificial intelligence continue to grow in scale, demand for electricity in data centers and cloud infrastructure is increasing, together with associated carbon emissions and water consumption. Recent studies by organizatio
content: As workloads in artificial intelligence continue to grow in scale, demand for electricity in data centers and cloud infrastructure is increasing, together with associated carbon emissions and water consumption. Recent studies by organizations such as the International Energy Agency and MIT indicate that AI-related electricity demand may rise sharply through 2030, creating important implications for energy systems and corporate sustainability strategies. This paper examines those implications from a cloud operations perspective rather than from the standpoint of hardware design or model research. The analysis argues that operational practices such as workload placement, energy-aware and carbon-aware scheduling, architectural right-sizing, stronger incident and capacity management, and cross-functional governance can materially reduce the environmental impact of AI-enabled infrastructure.

title: Data and materials for "Is AI-Augmented Customer Service Operationally Greener? A Scenario-Based Use-Phase Carbon Assessment of Human–AI Collaborative Service Systems"
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: This record provides the data and materials supporting a deterministic scenario-based comparison of provider-side use-phase operational electricity and associated carbon emissions across three customer-service architectures: traditional hum
content: This record provides the data and materials supporting a deterministic scenario-based comparison of provider-side use-phase operational electricity and associated carbon emissions across three customer-service architectures: traditional human service, a restricted-boundary pure-AI computational reference, and a human–AI Copilot architecture with class-specific escalation. The functional unit is 1,000 input tasks with an author-defined L1/L2/L3 workload mix. The deposit contains source-traceable numerical inputs, an explicit provenance register, author-defined scenario settings, a formula-driven Excel workbook, a standard-library Python implementation, reference results, a 690-row escalation/electricity-factor sensitivity matrix, eight parameter and boundary scenarios, 25 automated quality-assurance checks, and editable figure materials. This record contains no survey responses, human-participant data, customer records, personal identifiers, or confidential enterprise data. Third-party source documents are cited and linked but are not redistributed. The deposited values are conditional model estimates rather than enterprise measurements or a complete life-cycle assessment. Functional equivalence across the three service architectures has not been established. Data and non-code materials are licensed under CC BY 4.0, while the included Python code is licensed under the MIT License, as documented in the deposit.

title: Comments: Why Scaling CO2-EOR Remains Difficult
summary: _ In August, Occidental Petroleum told investors that Stratos, its long-awaited direct air capture (DAC) project, could be fully constructed by year-end, with full commercial operations expected in 2027. The Permian Basin facility, expected
content: _ In August, Occidental Petroleum told investors that Stratos, its long-awaited direct air capture (DAC) project, could be fully constructed by year-end, with full commercial operations expected in 2027. The Permian Basin facility, expected to be the world's largest DAC plant with a nameplate capacity of 500,000 metric tons of CO2per year, was initially targeted to begin operating in 2024. The startup date was later pushed to mid-2025, which ended up slipping once again. The company attributed the most recent setback to an unspecified component that required significant repairs but was said to be unrelated to the core DAC technology involved. The lengthy delay reflects not only the challenge of scaling emerging technologies such as DAC, but also serves as a general reminder of the often long and difficult process of integrating carbon capture, storage and utilization (CCUS) projects with oilfield operations. A point source for the emissions usually needs to be relatively close to the oil field to keep midstream costs manageable. Then there’s the cost of capturing technology, which can be expensive to install and maintain. In a low-price environment, justifying these added expenses can be too high a bar for management. Stratos is estimated to have cost Occidental and its partners $1.3 billion, which the company is hoping to make back by selling carbon credits to other industrial firms. It also wants to make money with the CO2by supporting its enhanced oil recovery (EOR) business in the Permian. The company has for decades used naturally sourced (i.e., geologic) CO2 for EOR in conventional rocks, but has recently committed to commercial-scale shale CO2-EOR. Occidental has outlined plans for three shale CO2-EOR projects, two in Texas and one in New Mexico, with additional developments hoped to come in the future. Early pilot results saw production gains of 40 to 50% above baseline levels, which represent a big enough carrot for the company to go after with new CO2 infrastructure. ExxonMobil is also looking to step up its CO2-EOR business following its 2023 acquisition of Denbury, which operated 1,300 miles of CO2pipelines across the US. The US supermajor has recently proposed a 900-mile "carbon superhighway" designed to transport captured shale CO2 from industrial facilities across Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi to other locations for EOR, permanent storage, and commercial beverage manufacturing. ExxonMobil has said CO2volumes and quality will be monitored as they enter and move through the system, likening the process to vehicles passing through toll booths. The US pioneered CO2-EOR in the 1970s and remains a global leader in the practice. There are more than 140 such projects spread across the country. This is according to a slightly dated report in 2021 from the Enhanced Oil Recovery Institute, which said then that CO2-EOR projects accounted for 273,000 B/D of combined output. But there are also projects outside of the US that are worth noting

title: co2gap — an open pipeline for measuring the CO2 of European flights against a fuel-optimal ideal, from ADS-B trajectories
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: A pipeline that reconstructs flight trajectories from open ADS-B archives and computes, for each flight, the CO2 actually emitted against that of an ideal trajectory: same aircraft type, direct great-circle route, fuel-optimal altitude and
content: A pipeline that reconstructs flight trajectories from open ADS-B archives and computes, for each flight, the CO2 actually emitted against that of an ideal trajectory: same aircraft type, direct great-circle route, fuel-optimal altitude and speed profile for the distance, and the same real wind from ERA5. The difference is decomposed into an additive lateral component (excess distance flown) and a vertical component (altitude and speed profile). Emissions are computed with OpenAP, with per-type correction factors anchored to the ICAO Carbon Emissions Calculator methodology. Results are aggregated by route and airport only, never per flight, aircraft or operator. Checked for consistency against the EUROCONTROL horizontal en-route flight efficiency indicator (KEA): the methodology states this is a consistency check, not a reproduction of their figure.

title: Technology Focus: Offshore Facilities (September 2026)
summary: _ Within the oil and gas industry, the arena of offshore facilities is subject to the same emphases and initiatives as its terrestrial counterpart. Decarbonization and automation have become focal points for marine structures and systems. T
content: _ Within the oil and gas industry, the arena of offshore facilities is subject to the same emphases and initiatives as its terrestrial counterpart. Decarbonization and automation have become focal points for marine structures and systems. This year’s selections, contributed to by reviewer Jefferson Couto, reflect an emphasis on emissions reduction and facilities repurposing for carbon capture, use, and storage (CCUS) projects as well as advances in automation and unattended operations. Paper SPE 37089 explores the application of a modular, high-temperature gas-cooled reactor to a Very Large Crude Carrier-class floating production, storage, and offloading vessel (FPSO). Highlighting a coherent case-study framework rather than detailed design optimization, the authors write that economics suggest that, for FPSOs burning associated gas, nuclear power remains disadvantaged in some aspects compared with gas turbines, but that a nuclear system’s associated, quantifiable emissions reductions, partially monetizable through carbon pricing and credit mechanisms, can offset a significant share of nuclear capital cost and make nuclear-powered FPSOs a credible decarbonization option for high-throughput offshore production. Combined-cycle power-generation technology, in which gas turbines and steam turbines are used together to convert fuel into electricity, is the focus of paper SPE 225466. The paper describes the potential of combined-cycle technology in CCUS applications for offshore facilities, especially when used in tandem with an exhaust-gas-recycling approach. The authors write that combined-cycle technology, which offers 22–25% reduced fuel consumption and CO2 emissions, is poised to make important strides into expanding offshore CCUS efforts. Finally, paper SPE 225805 discusses the process of assessing an aging offshore complex for the largest CCUS project in southeast Asia. Structural-integrity evaluations were used to check corrosion status as the platform nears the end of its design life. The paper uses the structural-integrity-management framework to evaluate the chosen platforms, highlighting their potential and limitations for CCUS purposes based on in-service assessments. The authors write that successful repurposing demands a demonstrated capacity to safely contain and manage new operational loads, resist CO2’s chemical and physical effects, and withstand cumulative aging for the entire service duration. Recommended papers highlight reuse of decommissioned facilities for CCUS, autonomous marine interventions, and a conceptual study for an unattended FPSO offshore Brazil.
